text: Some models only work well if all features are on a similar scale (for example 0–1). Which model does NOT care about the scale of the features?
explain: A tree asks questions like “is age > 30?”. Changing the units does not change which side of the line each point is on.

text: You have a column “city” with 30 different cities, in no particular order. How should you turn it into numbers for logistic regression?
options: Keep the city names as text
One column per city, with 1 or 0
explain: Numbering cities 0, 1, 2 pretends that one city is “bigger” than another. One 0/1 column per city (one-hot) avoids that.

text: Only 2 out of every 100 examples are “yes”. Your logistic regression just predicts “no” all the time. What is a good first fix?
options: Give the rare class more weight (class_weight='balanced')
explain: With weights, mistakes on the rare class cost more, so the model can no longer ignore it.

text: A sensor recorded values over time, but some values are missing. Which way of filling the gaps uses only values from the PAST?
options: Copy the last known value forward
Copy the next known value backward
Use the average of the whole series
Draw a line between the neighbours
explain: At prediction time you don’t know the future, so only “copy the last value” is fair.

text: You predict whether a patient has pneumonia when they arrive at the hospital. Which feature secretly gives away the answer (it would not exist yet at arrival)?
options: Whether they were given pneumonia medicine
explain: Medicine is given AFTER the diagnosis. Using it is cheating (called target leakage): the model looks great in testing but fails in real use.

text: In a dataset, 95% of the examples are “no”. A lazy model always answers “no”. What is its accuracy?
explain: It is right on every “no”, so 95%. High accuracy can mean nothing: always compare with this lazy baseline.

text: There are 100 real fraud cases. Your model raises 120 alarms, and 80 of the alarms are real fraud. Recall = how many of the real fraud cases did it find?
explain: It found 80 of the 100 real cases: recall = 80%. (Precision would be 80 of 120 alarms ≈ 67%.)

text: The model says “yes” when its probability is above 0.5. You lower this cut-off to 0.2. What usually happens?
options: Fewer false alarms, but it misses more real cases
It catches more real cases, but raises more false alarms
explain: With a lower cut-off the model says “yes” more often: more real cases found (recall up), more false alarms (precision down).

text: You predict house prices, and a few houses have crazy high prices. Which error measure is hurt LEAST by these few extreme houses?
explain: MSE squares each error, so one huge miss dominates. MAE just adds the sizes of the errors.

text: A classifier has ROC-AUC = 0.9. What does that mean?
options: A random “yes” example gets a higher score than a random “no” example 90% of the time
explain: ROC-AUC measures how well the model RANKS examples, over all possible cut-offs. It is not accuracy.

text: You try 200 different hyperparameter settings and keep the one with the best cross-validation score. How reliable is that best score?
options: It is exactly the test score
It is always lower than the test score
It is probably too optimistic; check on data you never used
explain: Picking the best of many noisy scores means some luck is included. Confirm on a held-out test set.

text: What does logistic regression give you for each example, before you decide “yes” or “no”?
options: The distance to the nearest point
explain: It computes a weighted sum and squashes it with the sigmoid into a probability.

text: Logistic regression uses an S-shaped curve (the sigmoid). Why is it still called a LINEAR classifier?
options: Because the sigmoid is a straight line
Because it is trained with squared error
Because it only works with one feature
Because the border between “yes” and “no” is a straight line
explain: It says “yes” exactly when the weighted sum is above 0, and that border is a straight line (a flat plane in more dimensions).

text: Class “yes” = all points inside a circle around (0, 0). A straight line can’t separate them. How can logistic regression still solve it?
options: Add the new features x² and y²
Number the x and y values 0, 1, 2…
explain: Inside the circle means x² + y² is small. With x² and y² as features, a straight-line rule works.

text: In linear regression, two features are almost exact copies of each other (for example height in cm and height in inches). What goes wrong?
options: The model can’t be trained at all
The weights become unstable and hard to interpret
explain: The model can split the weight between the twins in many ways. Predictions stay fine, but the weights jump around.

text: What is the main difference between a decision tree and a random forest?
options: A forest trains many trees on random parts of the data and combines their votes
A forest is one very deep tree
A forest can only predict numbers
explain: Each tree sees a random sample of rows and features; averaging many different trees makes fewer mistakes than one tree.

text: You train a decision tree with no depth limit. What usually happens?
options: It is too simple and misses patterns
It turns into a linear model
It memorises the training data and does worse on new data
explain: It keeps splitting until every training example is perfect: almost 100% on training data, worse on validation (overfitting).

text: When a decision tree splits the data into two groups, what is it trying to achieve?
options: Make each group as “pure” as possible (mostly one class)
Use the feature with the largest numbers
Make the two groups the same size
explain: It picks the question that best separates the classes (measured by Gini or entropy).

text: What is the difference between bagging and boosting?
options: Bagging trains models one after another; boosting trains them all at once
Bagging trains models independently; in boosting each new model fixes the previous ones’ mistakes
Boosting only works with linear models
explain: Bagging (e.g. random forest) averages independent models. Boosting (e.g. XGBoost) builds models in a row, each correcting the last.

text: You train gradient boosting. The validation error is lowest at 300 trees and then starts to grow. What should you do?
explain: After 300 trees the model starts memorising the training data. Early stopping keeps the best moment.

text: In a random forest, each split only looks at a random few of the features. Why?
options: It makes each single tree more accurate
So the features don’t need scaling
So the trees are different from each other and make different mistakes
explain: If all trees were the same, averaging would not help. Different trees make different mistakes that cancel out.

text: In gradient boosting (for predicting numbers), what does each NEW tree learn to predict?
options: The errors that the current model still makes (the residuals)
A random sample of the targets
explain: Each new tree learns “how far off are we still?”, and adding it corrects part of that error.

text: k-nearest neighbours with k = 1 classifies a point by copying its single closest neighbour. What tends to happen?
options: It overfits: every noisy point gets its own little region
It always draws a straight line
explain: One noisy neighbour decides everything. A larger k averages over more neighbours and smooths the border.

text: Naive Bayes is called “naive” because it assumes something simple. What?
options: That the features are independent of each other (within each class)
That all classes are equally common
That a straight line separates the classes
That there are no missing values
explain: It treats each feature as unrelated to the others, which is rarely true but often works well enough.

text: What does the “kernel trick” allow an SVM to do?
options: Draw curved borders without building the curved features by hand
explain: A kernel lets the SVM act as if it had many extra features (like x², xy…) without computing them, so the border can bend.

text: An SVM has a setting C (the penalty for mistakes on training data). What happens with a very LARGE C?
options: Wide margin, many training mistakes allowed
Narrow margin, it tries hard to get every training point right
The border becomes a straight line
explain: A big C punishes every training mistake heavily, so the model can overfit the training data.

text: What do you have to decide BEFORE you run k-means clustering?
options: The correct label of each point
explain: k-means needs the number of clusters in advance; you can try several and compare (for example with an elbow plot).

text: PCA finds new directions to describe the data. What is special about the FIRST direction it finds?
options: The data is most spread out along it
The data is least spread out along it
It points to the target label
It is always the first column
explain: The first direction keeps as much of the variation (spread) of the data as possible.

text: You run k-means twice on the same data and get different clusters. What is the most likely reason?
options: The starting cluster centres are chosen randomly
explain: The result depends on where the centres start. Run it several times (n_init) and keep the best.

text: Your data has two clusters shaped like bananas (moons), plus some random noise points. Which method fits it best?
explain: DBSCAN groups dense areas of any shape and marks lonely points as noise. k-means expects round blobs.

text: Training accuracy is 99%, validation accuracy is 70%. What is the problem?
options: The model memorised the training data (overfitting)
The validation set is too big
explain: A big gap between training and validation means overfitting: simplify, regularise, or get more data.

text: Regularisation adds a penalty for big weights. Which kind tends to make some weights exactly ZERO?
explain: L1 pushes unimportant weights all the way to 0, so it also selects features. L2 only makes weights smaller.

text: Training and validation scores are BOTH low and close to each other. What should you try?
options: A more powerful model or better features
explain: Both low means the model is too simple (underfitting). Give it more capacity or better features.

text: In scikit-learn’s LogisticRegression, what happens when you make C SMALLER?
explain: Careful: C is the opposite of regularisation strength. Small C = strong penalty = simpler model.

text: You scaled the training data with scaler.fit_transform(X_train). What should you run on the test data?
options: Nothing, test data is not scaled
explain: transform reuses the training data’s mean and std. Fitting again on the test data lets test information leak in.

text: In pandas, how do you count how many values are missing in each column of df?
explain: isna() marks every missing value as True, and sum() counts the Trues in each column.

text: To compute ROC-AUC for a yes/no model, which scikit-learn call gives you what you need?
explain: ROC-AUC needs the probability of “yes” for each example, not just the final 0/1 answers.

text: What does stratify=y do in train_test_split?
options: Keeps the same share of each class in the training and test parts
Sorts the rows by the label
explain: If 10% of the data is “yes”, both parts will also have about 10% “yes”. Important for small or unbalanced data.

text: Why put the scaler inside a Pipeline when you use cross-validation?
options: So the test folds are not scaled
So the scaler learns only from the training folds each time, with no peeking
explain: Scaling all the data first lets information from the validation folds leak in. In a Pipeline it is refit inside each fold.

text: Your one-hot encoder crashes because the test data contains a city it never saw in training. What is the simple fix?
options: Fit the encoder again on the test data
Number the cities in the test data only
explain: Unknown cities just get all zeros. Refitting on the test data would change which column means which city.
